author_claim: In Romans 10:11, Paul quotes directly from LXX Isaiah 28:16 and prefixes the pronoun πᾶς to emphasize the universal availability of salvation through faith in Christ.
short_quote: The universal aspect of the statement is emphasised by the pronoun ‘no one’ (πᾶς), which is missing from the quotation in Romans 9:33.
qualification: The pronoun πᾶς is absent from LXX Isaiah 28:16 and from Paul's earlier citation in Romans 9:33.
notes: Harmonizes with surrounding future-tense framework and prepares for Joel quotation in Rom 10:13.

author_claim: In Romans 10:11, Paul shifts the metaphorical meaning of the 'stone' in Isaiah 28:16 from a judge causing legalistic stumbling to the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection.
short_quote: The stone is no longer a judge but the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection.
qualification: Distinguishes the dual stumbling/firmness aspect of Rom 9:33 from the unmixed universal promise of Rom 10:11.
notes: Christological re-contextualization grounding justification by faith.

author_claim: Paul applies Isaiah's monotheistic statements in Isaiah 28:16 to both God the Father and Christ the Lord, presenting Christ as co-sovereign and co-unique with the Father.
short_quote: Paul is applying Isaiah’s monotheistic statements both to God and to Christ, the Lord, who is co-sovereign and co-unique with God the Father.
qualification: Both citations in Rom 9:33 and 10:11 are introduced by general references to Scripture rather than naming Isaiah directly.
notes: Cites Shum (2002) in fn. 40 on high Christology in Pauline Old Testament quotations.

author_claim: In Romans 9:33, Paul merges Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14 into a composite 'stone' quotation to show that trusting in works caused Israel to stumble over Christ, while faith yields certainty.
short_quote: This verse is a composite of two passages from Isaiah with the common theme of ‘stone’...
qualification: Scholarly debate noted between pre-Pauline oral/written testimonia (Koch, Dodd) and direct Pauline compilation from an Isaiah scroll in Corinth (Shum).

author_claim: The citation of Isaiah 28:16 in Romans 10:11 corresponds directly with the unmarked quotation of Joel 2:32 in Romans 10:13, united by πᾶς to establish faith as the universal criterion for salvation.
short_quote: The verse from Isaiah corresponds to the unmarked quotation from Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in Romans 10:13.
qualification: Joel 2:32 is cited without an introductory quotation formula, linked by catchword connection to Rom 10:11.
notes: Quotes Wilk (1998, 390) on Paul's commitment to the validity of the gospel for both Jew and Gentile.

author_claim: In Romans 11:34, Paul quotes almost word-for-word from LXX Isaiah 40:13 without an introductory formula, incorporating it into a hymn-like doxology expressing the unsearchable sovereignty of God.
short_quote: Without pointing it out, Paul quotes here almost word for word from Isaiah 40:13 – with a possible echo of Job 41:11 (LXX 41:3) – in a hymn-like doxology that expresses the greatness of God...
qualification: Paul quotes either from memory or by drawing on familiar biblical idiom without explicitly signaling a scriptural reference.
notes: Rounds off the theological discussion of Israel's election in Romans 9–11.

author_claim: Paul adapts Isaiah 40:13 selectively according to his contextual purpose, omitting the end of the verse in Romans 11:35 while omitting its middle section in 1 Corinthians 2:16.
short_quote: Elsewhere, in Romans 11:35, he omits the end of Isaiah 40:13; in 1 Corinthians 2:16, he leaves out the middle section.
qualification: Illustrates Paul's freedom of scriptural adaptation across differing epistolary contexts.
notes: Direct cross-epistle witness to Pauline quotation technique.

author_claim: In Romans 15:12, Paul places Isaiah 11:10 as the culmination of the citation chain in Romans 15:9–12, marking an ideological shift from general praise to the 'root of Jesse' as the hope of the Gentiles.
short_quote: There is something of a discontinuity – an ideological shift – between the quotations from Psalms/Deuteronomy and the verse from Isaiah. From explicit praise of the Lord, attention moves to the ‘root of Jesse’, who is the hope of the Gentiles.
qualification: Shifts focus from the internal community tension of the weak and strong to God's universal generosity in Christ.
notes: Introduced with the explicit formula Ἠσαΐας λέγει.

author_claim: Paul uses Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12 to present Jesus Christ as the promised messianic ruler over the nations who unites Jewish and Gentile believers in shared praise.
short_quote: Jesus Christ is the promised shoot from the stump of Jesse, the Messiah, the sovereign Lord, the ruler over the nations and the hope of salvation for the Gentiles; he is the Christ who ‘did not please himself’ (verse 3), who unites all people.
qualification: Provides positive motivation for mutual acceptance while preparing for Paul's concluding travel plans (Rom 15:14–33).
